scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. The user is asking if they're "AITA" (Are They the Asshole) for telling their mother that her being the reason they won't wear white to their wedding. 

First, I need to understand the scenario fully. The person is engaged and planning a small, semi-formal beach wedding. Their mother wants to go wedding dress shopping together at a specific bridal shop that only does white dresses. The person doesn't want a white dress and has already looked up the shop, knowing it's only white. They think the white dress tradition is silly, starting with Queen Victoria, and that the symbolism of purity and innocence is outdated. 

The main reason they don't want a white dress is that their mother wore white and got divorced. All other women in the family wore colored dresses and had long, mostly happy marriages. When the mother asked why they don't want white, the person first gave the Queen Victoria line, which the mother dismissed. Then they mentioned not being "innocent," which was an uncomfortable conversation. Finally, they admitted that the mother being the only one to break the tradition and get divorced made them not confident in white dresses. The mother got upset, cried, and said that the person spoke to her cruelly, knowing how the divorce affected her. The person hasn't apologized yet and feels the mother backed them into a corner, making them justify their choice when it's their wedding.

Now, I need to evaluate if the action of telling the mother the real reason is morally acceptable. 

On one hand, the person is making a personal choice about their wedding attire. It's their wedding, and they have the right to choose what they wear. They gave several valid reasons before revealing the personal one, which shows they tried to avoid the emotional topic. The mother's persistence in asking for the real reason might have forced the person to reveal something they preferred to keep private.

On the other hand, the person's choice to tie the mother's divorce and the tradition to their own wedding choice could be seen as insensitive. The mother might feel hurt that her past is being used as a reason for the person's decision, especially since it's a sensitive topic related to their divorce.

I also need to consider the context of family dynamics. The mother's reaction was emotional, and the person didn't apologize, which might have made the situation worse. However, the person feels that they shouldn't have to justify their choice, which is a valid point about personal autonomy.

In terms of morality, the action involves honesty but at the cost of hurting someone's feelings. It's a balance between being truthful and being considerate of others' emotions. While honesty is important, it's also crucial to communicate in a way that minimizes harm, especially with family members.

So, is the action morally acceptable? It's a tough call. The person had the right to choose their wedding attire and explain their reasons. However, the way they communicated the personal reason, especially in a way that linked the mother's past to their own choice, could be seen as insensitive. It's possible that a more tactful approach could have avoided the hurt feelings without compromising their choice.

Therefore, while the person's choice is valid, the manner in which they communicated their reasons might not be entirely morally acceptable because it caused emotional harm to their mother.
